nNeuron.title: Neuron
nNeuron.body:
The smallest part: multiply each input by a weight, add them up, add a bias, then pass the sum through a “switch” (the activation function).

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Neural Network Basics › Neuron
🔥 Has learnable parameters: adjusted in training, read-only in use
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • Output = activation(w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + … + b).
  • The weights decide “which input matters more, and whether it pushes up or down”
  • the bias sets “how high the bar is”.
  • On its own a neuron can only draw one straight line (or plane) through the input space.

🌱 Where it starts

Weights and bias start as small random numbers (see “Initialization”).

🔧 How training adjusts it

At every training step, backprop works out “how much the loss changes if this weight changes a little”, and the weights and bias move a little in the direction that lowers the loss.

▶ What it does in use

Weights are frozen; it just does the three steps: multiply, add, switch.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

  • Borrowed from the idea that a biological neuron “fires once it gets enough input”, but hugely simplified: only “weighted vote + threshold” is kept.
  • Simple enough to compute in bulk and to differentiate.

✅ Why this works

  • A weighted sum is matrix multiplication, which GPUs are extremely good at
  • every step is differentiable, so gradient descent can tune the weights automatically.
  • One neuron is weak, but thousands combined can express complex patterns.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Very different from real brain cells (no spike timing, no chemistry); “like a brain” is only a metaphor. A single neuron cannot learn XOR or anything that needs a curved boundary.

nLayer.title: A layer (fully connected)
nLayer.body:
Many neurons side by side, all looking at the same inputs, each giving one number.

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Neural Network Basics › A layer (fully connected)
🔥 Has learnable parameters: adjusted in training, read-only in use
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • A layer = one weight table (matrix) + a set of biases + an activation: output vector = activation(W·x + b).
  • Each neuron learns to “detect” one pattern.
  • The feed-forward network inside an LLM is exactly two such fully connected layers.

🌱 Where it starts

The weight table is randomly initialized; biases often start at 0.

🔧 How training adjusts it

The whole table is updated by gradients at once.

▶ What it does in use

One matrix multiplication computes the whole layer, all neurons in parallel.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

  • Putting many neurons in one layer lets a single matrix multiplication compute them all at once, which is what hardware does best
  • different random starting points make neurons naturally specialize in different patterns.

✅ Why this works

Each neuron draws one line, so a layer has many lines; after the activation “bends” them, the next layer can piece those bent lines into a curved boundary.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Wider layers mean more parameters and memory; a fully connected layer knows nothing about structure like “neighboring pixels” or “word order”, which is why convolution, attention and other structures exist.

nNet.title: Neural network
nNet.body:
Many layers stacked: each layer’s output is the next layer’s input.

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Neural Network Basics › Neural network
🔥 Has learnable parameters: adjusted in training, read-only in use
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • Input → layer 1 → layer 2 → … → output.
  • Each layer refines the last: early layers learn simple features, later layers combine them into complex ones.
  • An LLM is a very large neural network with a carefully designed structure (dozens of Transformer blocks stacked).

🌱 Where it starts

First fix the structure (how many layers, how wide), then randomly initialize every parameter.

🔧 How training adjusts it

The training loop: forward → loss → backprop → update, repeated many times.

▶ What it does in use

Parameters are frozen; only the forward pass runs.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

  • Instead of people writing rules, build a big “adjustable function” and let the data say where every knob should go.
  • Stacking layers is more parameter-efficient than one very wide layer: complex things are usually built from simpler ones.

✅ Why this works

  • In theory, a network with nonlinearities can approximate almost any function if it is big enough (the universal approximation theorem)
  • in practice, gradient descent on large networks usually finds parameters that work very well.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Universal approximation only says good parameters exist; it does not promise we can find them or that they will generalize. Why huge over-parameterized networks don’t overfit badly, and why gradient descent keeps finding good solutions, is still mostly empirical; theory does not fully explain it.

nFwd.title: Forward pass
nFwd.body:
Run the input through every layer to the output, giving the model’s answer (prediction).

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Neural Network Basics › Forward pass
⚙️ No learnable parameters: a fixed program / fixed rule / value computed on the fly
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

Each layer does “matrix multiply + bias + activation” and passes the result on. During training every layer’s intermediate results are kept, because backprop needs them.

🌱 Where it starts

A fixed procedure with no parameters of its own.

🔧 How training adjusts it

In training, the forward pass comes first and its intermediate results feed backprop.

▶ What it does in use

At use (inference) time only the forward pass runs, with no stored intermediates and no gradients, so it is far cheaper than training.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Split a complex function into simple layer-by-layer steps, each easy to compute and parallelize.

✅ Why this works

The same computation graph computes the answer and, walked backwards, the gradients; training and use share the same code.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Storing intermediates takes a lot of memory, one reason training costs far more than inference.

nLoss.title: Loss function
nLoss.body:
One number measuring “how far the model’s answer is from the right answer”. Smaller is better.

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Neural Network Basics › Loss function
⚙️ No learnable parameters: a fixed program / fixed rule / value computed on the fly
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • Regression usually uses mean squared error: (prediction − answer)²
  • classification usually uses cross-entropy: −log(probability given to the right answer).
  • An LLM’s “guess the next word” uses cross-entropy.

🌱 Where it starts

A formula chosen by people.

🔧 How training adjusts it

The “baton” of training: every parameter is pushed in the direction that makes it smaller.

▶ What it does in use

Not computed at use time (there is no right answer).

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

“How good” has to become one differentiable number, so gradient descent knows which way to go.

✅ Why this works

Cross-entropy punishes “confidently wrong” very hard, fits probability outputs naturally and has easy gradients, so classification and language models nearly all use it.

⚠️ Limits / notes: A low loss does not mean truly good: it only measures the goal you wrote down. Get the goal wrong and the model will optimize the wrong thing very well.

nBp.title: Backprop
nBp.body:
Walk back from the loss and use the chain rule to get every parameter’s gradient: “if it changes a little, how much does the loss change”.

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Neural Network Basics › Backprop
⚙️ No learnable parameters: a fixed program / fixed rule / value computed on the fly
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • Each node only needs its own “local derivative”.
  • Going backwards, it hands “gradient from upstream × local derivative” to the node before it, multiplying all the way back.
  • One backward pass gives the gradient of every parameter.

🌱 Where it starts

A fixed algorithm (deep-learning frameworks do it automatically: “autodiff”).

🔧 How training adjusts it

Done once at every training step.

▶ What it does in use

Not done at use time.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

  • There are billions of parameters
  • nudging them one at a time would need billions of forward passes.
  • The chain rule reuses intermediate results, so all gradients cost only about two forward passes’ worth of compute.

✅ Why this works

  • The gradient says exactly which direction and which parameters matter most.
  • This part is pure math (the chain rule) and always correct
  • what is uncertain is whether following the gradient leads somewhere good.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Gradients are multiplied layer after layer, so in deep networks they easily vanish or explode; that is why good activations, initialization, normalization and residuals matter. The brain probably does not learn this way.

nUpd.title: Update (gradient descent)
nUpd.body:
Every parameter takes a small step against its gradient: new = old − learning rate × gradient.

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Neural Network Basics › Update (gradient descent)
🔥 This is a training step: every parameter is changed here
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • The gradient points where the loss rises fastest, so stepping the other way lowers it.
  • The step size is the learning rate
  • in practice improved versions such as momentum and Adam are used (see “Optimizers”).
  • Using a small batch of data per step is called mini-batch stochastic gradient descent.

🌱 Where it starts

The optimizer’s hyperparameters (learning rate etc.) are set by people.

🔧 How training adjusts it

This step is what actually changes the model: every learnable parameter moves a little.

▶ What it does in use

No updates at use time.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

It decides where to go by the slope underfoot alone, without seeing the whole mountain; each step costs about as much as a forward pass, so it can repeat millions of times.

✅ Why this works

With small enough steps, each one lowers the loss a little; the random jitter from mini-batches empirically even helps escape bad spots and find solutions that generalize better.

⚠️ Limits / notes: It can stop in a local minimum or a flat region, and the learning rate needs tuning. Why it works so well on huge non-convex networks is not fully explained by theory yet.

nAct.title: Activation
nAct.body:
The “switch” or “bend” after the weighted sum: turns straight lines into kinks and curves.

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Neural Network Basics › Activation
⚙️ No learnable parameters: a fixed program / fixed rule / value computed on the fly
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

Common ones: step (early perceptrons, only 0/1), sigmoid (squeezes into 0–1), tanh (squeezes into −1–1), ReLU (negatives become 0, positives pass), GELU (a smooth ReLU, common in Transformers).

🌱 Where it starts

A fixed formula chosen by people (a few variants have learnable parameters).

🔧 How training adjusts it

Not trained itself, but its derivative decides whether gradients can flow back.

▶ What it does in use

Applied after every neuron’s weighted sum.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Without it, any number of layers equals one: a linear function of a linear function is still linear (W₂(W₁x) = (W₂W₁)x). Only with a “bend” do extra layers mean anything.

✅ Why this works

  • ReLU’s slope is exactly 1 on the positive side, so gradients flow back and it is cheap
  • that is why it quickly replaced sigmoid after 2012. Sigmoid’s slope is at most 0.25, so multiplying layer after layer makes it vanish.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Which is best is mostly decided by experiment (GELU and SwiGLU do slightly better in LLMs, without a complete theory why). ReLU neurons can “die” (stuck at 0, no longer learning).

nCg.title: Computation graph & chain rule
nCg.body:
Break the computation into small nodes joined in a graph; to differentiate, walk the graph backwards multiplying each local derivative.

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Neural Network Basics › Computation graph & chain rule
⚙️ No learnable parameters: a fixed program / fixed rule / value computed on the fly
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

For example z = w·x + b, a = σ(z), L = ½(a − t)². The chain rule: ∂L/∂w = ∂L/∂a × ∂a/∂z × ∂z/∂w. Each node only handles its own small derivative; combined they give the whole chain.

🌱 Where it starts

Recorded automatically by the framework during the forward pass.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Walked backwards at every training step.

▶ What it does in use

Only walked forwards at use time.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

  • Write the derivative of each small operation (add, multiply, exp…) once, and any complex model built from them can be differentiated automatically
  • researchers never derive formulas by hand.

✅ Why this works

The chain rule guarantees exact results; going backwards, each “upstream gradient” is shared by everything below it, avoiding enormous repeated work.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Only works for differentiable operations; discrete choices (sampling, rounding) need approximation tricks.

nOpt.title: Optimizers: SGD / momentum / Adam
nOpt.body:
The rule for “exactly how to step once you have the gradient”.

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Neural Network Basics › Optimizers: SGD / momentum / Adam
⚙️ No learnable parameters: a fixed program / fixed rule / value computed on the fly
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • SGD: step straight against the gradient.
  • Momentum: remember previous directions, like a ball rolling downhill with inertia, so it stops zig-zagging in narrow valleys.
  • Adam: on top of momentum, scale each parameter’s step by how big its recent gradients were—small steps where it is steep, bigger where it is flat.
  • LLM training mostly uses Adam and variants (such as AdamW).

🌱 Where it starts

Chosen by people; the “memory” inside momentum and Adam starts at 0.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Turns gradients into parameter updates at every step.

▶ What it does in use

Not needed at use time.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

  • Real loss landscapes are long narrow valleys, plateaus and saddle points
  • plain SGD is either slow or wobbly there.
  • Inertia and adaptive step sizes are targeted fixes for that terrain.

✅ Why this works

Momentum averages out back-and-forth components and accumulates consistent ones; Adam keeps every parameter’s step on a similar scale, so each layer needs no separate learning rate.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Adam stores two extra numbers per parameter (more memory); which optimizer is best depends on the task, and many conclusions are empirical.

nLr.title: Learning rate
nLr.body:
How big each step is. One of the most important hyperparameters.

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Neural Network Basics › Learning rate
⚙️ No learnable parameters: a fixed program / fixed rule / value computed on the fly
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • Too small: crawls, never reaching the bottom.
  • Too big: overshoots the bottom, bounces back and forth, or climbs ever higher (diverges).
  • Real training often “warms up” from small to large, then slowly decays (a learning-rate schedule).

🌱 Where it starts

Set by people, often found with small experiments.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Changes on a schedule during training.

▶ What it does in use

Not present at use time.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

The gradient gives direction and slope, not how far to go; the closer to the bottom, the smaller the steps should be.

✅ Why this works

Within the right range, a larger rate moves fast and can hop out of small pits; lowering it later lets training settle steadily.

⚠️ Limits / notes: The best value depends on model size, batch size and optimizer, and is mostly found by experience and trial.

nBatch.title: Mini-batches & epochs
nBatch.body:
Each update uses only a small batch of examples; one pass over all the data is an epoch.

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Neural Network Basics › Mini-batches & epochs
⚙️ No learnable parameters: a fixed program / fixed rule / value computed on the fly
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • Say 10,000 images in batches of 100: one epoch = 100 updates.
  • Bigger batches give more accurate gradients but cost more per step
  • smaller batches update more often but are noisier.
  • LLM training data is so large that it is usually seen only about once.

🌱 Where it starts

Batch size and number of epochs are set by people.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Determines how training proceeds step by step.

▶ What it does in use

At use time several requests are often grouped into one batch (a different sense of “batching”).

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Computing the gradient over all data is too expensive; a small batch’s average gradient is already a decent estimate, and it lets you update far more often.

✅ Why this works

The estimate’s error shrinks as batches grow (roughly with the square root); a moderate amount of noise even acts as regularization in practice.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Very large batches can generalize worse and need learning-rate retuning; there is no universal formula for the best size.

nSplit.title: Train / validation / test sets
nSplit.body:
Split data three ways: one to learn from, one to tune settings and decide when to stop, one kept for a single final exam.

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Neural Network Basics › Train / validation / test sets
⚙️ No learnable parameters: a fixed program / fixed rule / value computed on the fly
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • Common splits are 70% / 15% / 15% or 80% / 10% / 10%.
  • Parameters update only on the training set
  • the validation set compares learning rates, depths and so on and drives early stopping
  • the test set stays untouched until the final score.

🌱 Where it starts

Divided by people before training.

🔧 How training adjusts it

The training set drives updates; the validation set only checks.

▶ What it does in use

The test set simulates “real situations never seen before”.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Models memorize the questions they have seen. Scored only on training data, a model that memorized answers gets full marks; only unseen questions reveal whether it really learned.

✅ Why this works

  • All three come from the same distribution, so validation performance is an unbiased estimate of real performance
  • using the test set only once avoids “tuning until you have effectively peeked at the answers”.

⚠️ Limits / notes: If test questions leak into training data (contamination), scores are inflated—a frequent problem with public LLM benchmarks.

nInit.title: Initialization
nInit.body:
The small random numbers given to every weight before training starts.

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Neural Network Basics › Initialization
⚙️ No learnable parameters: a fixed program / fixed rule / value computed on the fly
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • They cannot all be 0 (every neuron would be identical and learn the same thing forever)
  • the random scale is set by layer width, e.g. variance about 1/number of inputs (Xavier / He initialization), so every layer’s output has a similar size.

🌱 Where it starts

Generated randomly by a rule.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Only sets the starting point; training changes it afterwards.

▶ What it does in use

Use time uses the trained values.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Randomness breaks symmetry so neurons specialize; the right scale keeps signals and gradients from exploding or vanishing across dozens of layers.

✅ Why this works

Scaling by width keeps each layer’s “total input” at the same order of magnitude, so a deep network starts in a trainable state.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Good initialization only gets training started; with normalization and residuals, deep networks are much less sensitive to it.

nNorm.title: Normalization (basics)
nNorm.body:
Pull a layer’s numbers back to a standard size so they don’t keep growing or shrinking.

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Neural Network Basics › Normalization (basics)
🔥 Partly learnable: only a small set of numbers is adjusted by training
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • BatchNorm (looks across a batch) is common in image networks
  • LayerNorm / RMSNorm (looks across one example’s own numbers) is common in Transformers.
  • A set of learnable scale numbers is then applied.

🌱 Where it starts

Scale numbers usually start at 1.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Only the scale (and offset) numbers are trained.

▶ What it does in use

Computed in every layer as usual.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

The more layers, the easier the scale drifts; recalibrating each layer means later layers always see similar-sized inputs.

✅ Why this works

Stable scales allow larger learning rates and faster, steadier training; exactly why it works so well has several competing explanations.

⚠️ Limits / notes: BatchNorm depends on batch size and does not suit word-by-word generation, one reason Transformers use LayerNorm/RMSNorm.

nReg.title: Regularization
nReg.body:
Ways to discourage rote memorization: L2 weight decay, dropout, early stopping, more data.

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Neural Network Basics › Regularization
⚙️ No learnable parameters: a fixed program / fixed rule / value computed on the fly
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • L2: add “sum of squared weights × a coefficient” to the loss so weights prefer to stay small and curves stay smooth.
  • Early stopping: watch the validation loss and stop when it no longer improves, keeping the best parameters.
  • Data augmentation: flip and crop images to create more practice examples.

🌱 Where it starts

Coefficients are set by people.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Only has an effect during training.

▶ What it does in use

No extra work at use time (dropout is off).

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

When there are enough parameters to memorize every training point, the model fits the noise; regularization rewards simpler explanations.

✅ Why this works

Real patterns are usually smoother and more consistent than noise; preferring small weights and smooth curves makes catching the pattern more likely than catching the noise.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Too strong and it underfits; huge models trained about once over huge data face quite different overfitting risks than small models.

nDrop.title: Dropout
nDrop.body:
During training, randomly switch off part of the neurons (say half) at every step; at use time all are on.

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Neural Network Basics › Dropout
⚙️ No learnable parameters: a fixed program / fixed rule / value computed on the fly
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • A switched-off neuron outputs 0 for that step and the rest are scaled up to keep the total.
  • A different set is dropped every step, like training many smaller networks that share parameters.

🌱 Where it starts

The drop rate is set by people.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Random dropping happens only in training.

▶ What it does in use

No dropping at use time, so results are deterministic.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

No single neuron is allowed to become irreplaceable, forcing the network to spread and back up information.

✅ Why this works

Roughly averages many sub-networks, and averages are usually steadier and overfit less (an empirical finding with partial theory).

⚠️ Limits / notes: It slows training; many LLMs skip dropout in pre-training because there is so much data.

nCnn.title: Convolutional network (CNN)
nCnn.body:
Slide one small “filter” (kernel) across the image to find patterns, combining layer by layer: edges → textures → parts → objects.

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Neural Network Basics › Convolutional network (CNN)
🔥 Has learnable parameters: adjusted in training, read-only in use
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • A kernel is a small patch of weights (say 3×3) computed at every position as “multiply cell by cell, then add”
  • the same kernel is reused everywhere (weight sharing).
  • Pooling shrinks the image so later layers see a wider area.

🌱 Where it starts

Kernels are randomly initialized.

🔧 How training adjusts it

The numbers in the kernels are trained and learn to find useful patterns themselves.

▶ What it does in use

Parameters frozen, slid across the image.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

  • In images “a pattern means the same wherever it appears” and “neighboring pixels are most related”.
  • Building these two facts into the structure means far fewer parameters and much faster learning.

✅ Why this works

Weight sharing makes what one kernel learns valid across the whole image; stacking layers widens the view, naturally forming a local-to-global hierarchy.

⚠️ Limits / notes: With enough data, vision Transformers (ViT) often match or beat CNNs; today the two are often combined.

nRnn.title: Recurrent neural network (RNN)
nRnn.body:
Reads one word at a time, updating a “memory” (hidden state) after each, then carries it to the next word.

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Neural Network Basics › Recurrent neural network (RNN)
🔥 Has learnable parameters: adjusted in training, read-only in use
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

h_t = f(W·h_(t−1) + U·x_t + b): the same weights are reused at every time step. Unrolled in time it is a very deep network, one layer per word.

🌱 Where it starts

Weights randomly initialized; memory starts at 0.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Weights trained with backpropagation through time (BPTT).

▶ What it does in use

Reads the input step by step, then generates step by step.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Sentences vary in length; reusing one small network handles any length without more parameters.

✅ Why this works

The hidden state compresses everything read so far into a fixed-size vector carried forward; it suits speech and short text.

⚠️ Limits / notes: ① Each word must wait for the previous one, so it cannot be parallelized and trains slowly; ② early information must pass through many steps to reach later ones, fading along the way, and gradients vanish; ③ everything is squeezed into one fixed-size vector. These three points are exactly why the Transformer replaced it.

nLstm.title: LSTM
nLstm.body:
An RNN with “gates”: switches decide what to keep in memory, what to forget and what to output.

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Neural Network Basics › LSTM
🔥 Has learnable parameters: adjusted in training, read-only in use
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • It has a “memory conveyor belt” (the cell state) along which information can travel almost unchanged
  • forget, input and output gates (sigmoids between 0 and 1) control reading and writing.
  • Proposed in 1997, it powered machine translation and speech recognition in the mid-2010s.

🌱 Where it starts

Weights randomly initialized; the forget-gate bias is often set high so it starts out “remembering”.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Trained like an RNN, through time.

▶ What it does in use

Reads and writes step by step.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

A plain RNN’s memory is multiplied at every step and fades fast; on the conveyor belt information is added and subtracted rather than multiplied, so it survives long distances.

✅ Why this works

Gates let the network learn how long to remember, and gradients travel further along the belt (the same idea as residual connections).

⚠️ Limits / notes: Forgetting is eased, but it still computes step by step, cannot be parallelized, and still struggles with very long text.

nEmb.title: Word vectors
nEmb.body:
Each word gets a list of numbers (a vector); words with similar meanings get nearby vectors.

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Neural Network Basics › Word vectors
🔥 Has learnable parameters: adjusted in training, read-only in use
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • Training pulls together the vectors of words that appear in similar contexts (the word2vec idea).
  • Directions between vectors sometimes carry relations: “king − man + woman” lands near “queen”.
  • An LLM’s embedding table is a big table like this, whose vectors attention later rewrites by context.

🌱 Where it starts

Random initialization.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Trained along with every other parameter.

▶ What it does in use

Looked up to get each word’s vector.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Computers only compute numbers; give every word an unrelated ID and the model cannot see that “cat” and “dog” are alike. With vectors, similarity becomes “being close”.

✅ Why this works

Training to guess words from context forces words that appear in the same places to get similar vectors, so meaning and grammar emerge as geometry (an empirical observation).

⚠️ Limits / notes: Analogies only hold roughly, and vectors also learn the data’s biases (such as stereotyped job–gender links). Real vectors have hundreds to thousands of dimensions; any 2D picture distorts them.

xgen.title: Autoencoders, VAEs and GANs
xgen.body:
The prequel to today’s image generators: learn to compress data into a few numbers, or learn to produce samples that look real.

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Neural Network Basics › Autoencoders, VAEs and GANs
🔥 A trained capability: learned from data in training, read-only at use time

🎯 Role

  • Autoencoder: an encoder squeezes the input into a small z and a decoder reconstructs it; the closer the better.
  • VAE: the encoder outputs a distribution and samples z = μ + σ·ε (the reparameterisation trick) so everything trains with gradients; the objective is reconstruction error plus a KL term pulling z towards a standard normal.
  • GAN: a generator G makes samples from noise, a discriminator D judges real or fake, and the two train against each other.

▶ How to use it

  • To see its role in today’s image generation, drill down to the VAE popup on the multimodal and generation station.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Learning the probability of “what images look like” directly is too hard; compressing to a few numbers, or pitting two networks against each other, sidesteps it.

✅ Why this works

The GAN paper proves that at the optimum the generated distribution equals the data distribution and the discriminator outputs 1/2 everywhere; its own analogy is counterfeiters versus police.

⚠️ Limits / notes: A GAN must keep G and D in sync, or G maps many noise vectors to the same sample (mode collapse); it gives no explicit probability either.
